_readme: Every module at this repo's root MUST have an entry here, and CI fails if one does not —
including modules that own nothing. An explicit empty `resources` with a `why` is a decision;
a missing entry is an oversight, and the two must not look the same.
`resources` lists the external things this module OWNS: the table it writes, the endpoint it
calls. Consumers register these in their own .shared-resources.json, which is what makes the
inlining gate able to see a re-implementation. check-resource-registration.mjs compares the two
and fails a consumer that imports a module without registering its resources.
Match the OPERATION, not the name. A rule that fires on a legitimate read of a table this module
writes is a rule people learn to skim past.

adPlatforms.why: NOT expressible as a resource match, and the attempt is worth recording. A rule on the platform hostnames was tried and flagged 17 sites across 11 repos, every one legitimate: the cookie-banner component (deliberately per-repo, because brand styling differs — and it is what actually loads the tags), the CSP host lists this module exports constants for, and Playwright assertions naming the hosts they expect to be absent before consent. The real contract here — 'adding a platform is ONE entry in AD_PLATFORMS' — is about where a REGISTRY ENTRY goes, not about who may name a hostname. A gate cannot see that distinction, and a rule firing on 17 correct sites is one people would disable. Enforced by review and by repo CLAUDE.md instead.

admin.why: takes a caller-supplied client and answers an owner-tier question. The privilege rule itself lives once, in the DB (see the auth/admin standard) — this module owns no external resource of its own.

alerting.why: a pure decision function: it is handed the current failures plus the previous state and returns which are new. It reads and writes nothing — the caller chooses where to persist the returned state (a heartbeat row, a JSON file), because that store is the caller's, not this module's. No resource match was added: the thing worth forbidding is hand-rolled alert suppression, and that has no reliable textual signature — any regex broad enough to catch it would fire on every ordinary comparison against a timestamp. Enforced by review and by the estate alert-quality standard instead. Note this module has a deliberate Node/CommonJS twin outside this repo for the scheduled agents, which cannot import TypeScript; the two must change together and this file is the canonical spec.

resources.reason: an audit row written by hand can skip the shared action slugs and the request-context parsing, producing rows that look valid and cannot be correlated. Reading audit_log is fine.
the BartMail HTTP API must never be called — optins are a direct Supabase write through this module. Standing rule, predates the module.

a contact_tags write can SEND EMAIL: the AFTER INSERT trigger feeds tag_enrolment_outbox, matched on tag name + tenant, NOT brand. Hand-writing this is how a bulk tool fires an unrelated brand's sequence.

charts.why: pure number/currency formatting. No external system, nothing to own.

resources.reason: consent must persist in a cookie scoped to the registrable domain. localStorage is keyed by ORIGIN, so a localStorage-backed banner re-prompts on every subdomain — including a checkout mid-payment.

consentBannerSize.why: owns a THRESHOLD and a measurement, not an external system — there is nothing to write to and nothing to call. The re-implementation worth forbidding is a spec that retypes the percentage instead of importing it, and that is not a resource match: it is caught by scripts/check-consent-banner-size.mjs, which requires the constant to arrive via an import from this module and fails a spec that merely names the same number.

deadSpace.why: owns a MEASUREMENT and its thresholds (gap px limits, flat-band texture stddev, empty-box height), not an external system. Added 2026-10-06 (estate issue 74cbe86c) so every repo's tests/mobile.spec.ts calls one auditDeadSpace() instead of pasting a 270-line copy, which is what the starter template carried from 2026-10-01 and why the check reached no other repo. No resource match: the re-implementation risk is a pasted scanDeadSpace/bandTextureStddev in a spec, which has no stable textual signature; enforced by review, same as consentBannerSize.

resources.reason: three repos each grew their own writeHeartbeat inside lib/cron.ts; two drifted on updated_at and nothing noticed, because no file was named cronHeartbeat.ts for the filename gate to catch. Matches the WRITE only — the status dashboard and staleness watcher read it legitimately.

the per-run history row is written by the same module as the heartbeat, and for the same reason — an inline copy drifts on the duration/started_at handling and, worse, on the never-throws contract. Matches the WRITE only: a history view and a retention sweep read and delete it legitimately.

deposit.why: pure arithmetic over line items and a caller-supplied rule. Owns no external system. It is here because the figure is computed on both the document a customer signs and the invoice raised from it, and two implementations disagreeing means asking for one amount and billing another — which happened. Every value that decides an outcome (percentages, threshold, which categories are payable in full) is passed in, so no commercial policy lives in this repo.

resources.reason: send pacing, the 2/sec API cap and retry handling live in this module. A direct call bypasses all three and can trip the rate limit for every other sender.

emailit.why: Owns the transactional send transport AND the provider's per-address suppression switch (the delivery gate, never an audience). clearSelfRequestedSoftFailSuppression() is the ONE implementation of 'a person just asked for mail, so a soft-fail suppression on that exact address is cleared first' — soft-fail only, hard/complaint/unsubscribe never touched, fail-closed on its audit+throttle store. Before it existed a soft-fail suppression from a months-old deferral silently swallowed sign-in codes and purchase receipts, with the provider accepting the API call and dropping the mail. Also owns the BUYER'S-OWN-ADDRESS check for a success page (checkBuyerDeliverability: soft = nothing, hard bounce = warn, complaint = one-click opt-in; bounded to 1.5s, fails soft) and clearComplaintSuppressionOnConsent(), the ONE way a COMPLAINT suppression is ever removed: only on the buyer's own explicit click (the flag is a literal-true parameter), audited with the order, throttled, never a hard bounce, and never paired with a marketing tag or list write (a tag write can start a sequence that sends email). classifySuppression() is the single place that decides soft/hard/complaint/unsubscribe.

resources.reason: the shared client carries retry handling a hand-rolled token fetch does not. NOTE: one consumer keeps a deliberate local graph.ts (Drafts support the shared module lacks) — that repo allow-lists it rather than pretending otherwise.

jsonLd.why: pure escaping before embedding structured data in a script tag. No external system.

resources.reason: a consumer file mapping specific mailbox domains (gmail.com, hotmail.com, icloud.com, ...) to a provider string is a hand-rolled copy of MAIL_PROVIDER_DOMAINS, and it drifts the moment this module's list is extended (a new consumer domain, a provider consolidation) without the consumer noticing. At least one consumer already carries a local MX-based provider lookup that predates this module (2026-09-08); it registers this resource in its own `.shared-resources.json` with an `allow` entry for its own path until migrated onto this module, rather than the pattern being blocked outright here.

an MX lookup outside this module has no timeout race and no in-memory cache, and reimplements the suffix-matching providerFromMxHosts owns — three ways to get the same lookup subtly wrong. Same pre-existing consumer and same grandfathering note as above; new callers should go through detectMailProvider.

mailProviderDomains.why: MAIL_PROVIDER_DOMAINS and the sync detectMailProviderFromDomain — split out of mailProvider.ts on 2026-09-08 so a client component can do domain-map-only provider detection (no MX fallback available) with zero risk of pulling in the lazy `node:dns` import that file carries for MX lookups. The domain-map resource-detection pattern (a hand-rolled copy of MAIL_PROVIDER_DOMAINS, or a raw dns.resolveMx call) is declared once under the `mailProvider` entry above and covers this file too — same list, same drift risk, just relocated. mailProvider.ts re-exports this whole file, so the public surface is unchanged.

mailProviderEvents.why: fires the post-submit deliverability notice's analytics signal (a gtag event, when the site's own gtag already exists, plus a `post-submit-notice` CustomEvent on window regardless). No external system of its own — it only reads `window.gtag` if present and dispatches a DOM event. No imports at all beyond types from mailProviderNotice.ts, deliberately, so a client component can import it directly with zero risk of pulling in mailProvider.ts's lazy `node:dns` dependency.

mailProviderNotice.why: the MailProvider type, the isMailProvider guard, the `?p=` query-param helpers, and the post-submit deliverability notice copy — split out of mailProvider.ts on 2026-09-08 so a client component can import it with zero risk of pulling in the lazy `node:dns` import that file carries for MX lookups. Pure copy and string formatting; owns no external system. mailProvider.ts re-exports this whole file, so the public surface is unchanged.

resources.reason: the CAPI events edge only — other Graph edges (/insights, /stats, ad and audience management) are not this module’s and are deliberately not matched. A hand-rolled POST here re-creates four things that took a while to get right: SHA-256 lower-cased/trimmed hashing of email and first name, the `fb.1.<ts>.<fbclid>` fbc derivation that is the whole point of the server path (it survives a consent decline), the shared `eventId` that stops server and browser double-counting the same event, and the error-logging rule — Meta echoes request context back inside `error.message`, so this module logs status and numeric code/type ONLY, never the message and never the body, which carries the access token and hashed PII. It also swallows failures after logging, because a tracking write must never fail the page or the payment that called it.

a page-view-shaped CAPI event must go through sendLandingPageView, which refuses automated requests. Building one by hand with sendCAPIEvent skips that gate. On 2026-09-08 a server-side ViewContent was added to a landing page inside after(); the page was force-dynamic, so every crawler, link-scraper and prefetch rendered it and fired the event too. Server-side ViewContent on that pixel went from about 1/hour to 267, 333 and 230 in single hours — a twentyfold inflation of the exact event the live ad sets were optimising on, so real money was spent teaching Meta to find traffic that looks like a crawler. Purchase, Lead and other webhook-driven events are NOT matched: those have no browser request behind them and the gate would be meaningless there.

metaClickEvent.why: the pure half of the server twin of a click event (AddToCart, InitiateCheckout, Lead...): the click-event allowlist (never ViewContent/PageView, which a crawler can emit), the body parser with the mandatory shared event id, and the fail-closed origin check. Owns no external system — the events edge it feeds is matched under metaCapi above. Split out so the rules can be unit-tested; sendClickEvent in metaCapi imports server-only, which cannot resolve in the node:test build.

metaCapiUserData.why: the pure half of metaCapi: Meta's customer-information normalisation and SHA-256 hashing (em, fn, ln, ph with country code, country, external_id) plus fbc rebuilt from a stored click id at its click time. Owns no external system — the events edge it feeds is matched under metaCapi above, which is where a hand-rolled send would be caught. Split out so the hashing rules can be unit-tested; metaCapi imports server-only, which cannot resolve in the node:test build.

nextRedirects.why: Owns no external resource — it is a list of Next.js redirect rules, consumed by next.config.ts via a RELATIVE import, because the Next config loader does not resolve tsconfig path aliases. A resource match is also the wrong tool here: the thing worth enforcing is that every site SPREADS SHARED_REDIRECTS, which is an ABSENCE, and the inlining gate can only see presence. That check lives in each consumer instead — if public/ holds any .md, next.config.ts must import SHARED_REDIRECTS. Live verification is separate again, in the security-audit agent, because a config that exists is not proof of a config that works.

resources.reason: the printable-ASCII range literal is the signature of a hand-rolled sanitiser for the standard PDF fonts, and every local copy so far failed the same way: it DROPPED what it could not encode, which silently deletes a ✓ prefixing a list item — the document still renders, so nothing reports it. Worse, a copy applied to wrapped body text only leaves the short single-line draw sites unguarded, and the library throws from measurement as well as drawing, so one stray glyph in a title fails the whole render. Matched on the RANGE, not on the code-page name: the name appears in ordinary prose and comments, and a rule that fires on those is one people learn to skim past.

postgrestFilters.why: pure string functions over a filter grammar. Owns no external system, so there is nothing to resource-match — the re-implementation risk is covered mechanically instead, by scripts/check-postgrest-filter-terms.mjs, which fails any interpolation of a term into a like/ilike filter that does not route through this module. That gate is the resource match for this one.

resources.reason: the shared module is fail-open and applies the spamtrap rule. A direct call can accept addresses this one blocks, and burns the 4,300/day account-wide credit cap.

a hand-rolled sanitise call drifts from the shared forbid-lists, and silently deletes embedded ld+json schema unless the caller reimplements the extract-validate-reattach carve-out — which two consumers had each written separately, one of them noting in a comment that it mirrored the other. Sanitisers with no jsdom dependency (sanitize-html, remark-html's own sanitize) are a DIFFERENT operation for a different runtime constraint and are deliberately not matched here.

safeHtmlNoDom.why: the jsdom-free twin of safeHtml, for serverless and edge runtimes where the DOMPurify/jsdom chain throws at module load. Deliberately NO resource match on `sanitizeHtml(`: a direct sanitize-html call is not a re-implementation of this module, it is the same primitive this module wraps, and at least one consumer route calls it directly for exactly the runtime reason this module exists — a gate firing on that would flag the correct code. What must not be re-implemented is the extract-validate-reattach ld+json carve-out, which has no reliable textual signature; the safeHtml entry's DOMPurify match already covers the version of that mistake a gate can see.

security.why: crypto and comparison primitives operating on caller-supplied values. Its security comes from the keys it is given, never from what it talks to.

resources.match: iabjs:|Java object is gone|Object Not Found Matching Id|translate_http
resources.reason: these are the fingerprints of third-party scripts injected into a page the app did not write — an in-app-browser bridge, an extension's DOM walker, a translation proxy. They have no reason to appear in application code for ANY other purpose, so a file naming one is a hand-rolled copy of this module's filter. That copy is what the module exists to stop: at consolidation the estate had three filter families spread over the repos, not one repo carried all three, and the iOS and Android halves of the SAME in-app-browser bug had each been found and filtered in a different repo with neither aware of the other. Deliberately NOT matching `window.webkit.messageHandlers` (a plausible legitimate feature-detect for native bridging) or `NEXT_REDIRECT` (legitimately named in middleware and tests) — a gate that fires on correct code is one people learn to skim past.
search logging and article writes share ranking assumptions with the reader; a second writer drifts them apart silently.

resources.why: A site must NOT write a support ticket itself. BartMail owns the pipeline, and the spam gate (denylist, allowlist, AI sender classification, daily cost cap) runs there — a direct insert skips all of it and fills the helpdesk with the rubbish the gate exists to stop. This module POSTs to BartMail's /api/support/form-ticket instead. Matches the WRITE: the helpdesk app reads and updates these rows constantly and legitimately.

Same reason, plus one specific trap the endpoint handles: the body goes in body_text, never body_html. A contact form is public input, and a site writing it as HTML turns its own form into a stored-XSS path into the agent console.

resources.reason: a hand-rolled Telegram post skips the delivery check — the API answers 200 with {ok:false} for some errors and 404 for a revoked token, both of which resolve the promise happily — and skips the 4096-character cap, where an over-long alert is rejected entirely rather than truncated. Both failure modes are silent, on the channel whose whole job is to be heard when the primary one is not.

buyerContact.why: pure copy and classification for the human hand-off when a buyer's email is blocked: a complaint becomes a personal Outlook DRAFT (never auto-sent) carrying their ticket code, a hard bounce becomes a Command Centre task and bell with every other contact detail. Does no I/O; the apps own the Graph draft and the bell call.

ownAddress.why: the buyer's own-address banner copy and the one-click complaint opt-in, as pure logic over injected I/O. The order of its steps is the safety (re-check that it is still a complaint, claim the single per-order use, clear, only then resend) and its deps have no marketing member at all, so a tag, list or suppression write is not expressible. Every app's success page calls this so the wording and the rules cannot drift.

safetyNet.why: pure content for the 'everything you need without the email' block on a success page: the order ref, a code or link where the product has one, the steps, the support line, and the copy-details text, for every product type (game licence, course, download, physical, none, unknown). One model feeds the page, the PDF ticket and the copy text so they cannot disagree. Product- and brand-neutral: names, URLs and the support address are passed in. The page component stays per-repo (no React here); scripts/check-success-safety-net.mjs gates that a payment-confirming success page renders it.

prepaidRedeem.why: the thin server-side client a site uses to add a 'Redeem a code' box: tidy/plausibility helpers, the same-for-every-refusal wording, and one function that asks the checkout app (hostname, shared service token and the end user's IP all passed in by the caller) to redeem a code and returns where to send the buyer. Every rule (existence, single use, expiry, rate limit, fulfilment) lives in the checkout app that owns the codes, never here. No resource is registered because the endpoint belongs to the checkout app, whose own handler is the single implementation; a consumer re-implementing the call would still have to hold the shared service token, which only the sites meant to call it do.

ticketPdf.why: a hand-written one-page PDF (standard fonts, WinAnsi, optional QR matrix passed in) for the safety-net ticket. No library and no network, so it adds no dependency to any consumer. The route that serves it holds a bearer code and must send Cache-Control private, no-store after authorising the caller.

resources.reason: the checkout service's public gift-availability endpoint. It sends no CORS headers, so it must be called server-side with a short timeout and a safe false on any failure; hand-rolling the call re-implements the https/slug validation and the never-throw contract. The gift checkout link (?gift=1) is built by giftCheckoutUrl for the same reason.

uploads.why: MIME sniffing, filename safety and size validation on bytes the caller already holds. It talks to nothing; the storage client stays in the consuming app.

resources.reason: a hand-written map of mistyped provider domains is a copy of suggestEmailCorrection() that drifts the first time a provider or a false positive (mail.com is not a typo of gmail.com) is added. Call the shared function.

validation.why: pure predicates over strings. No external system. Includes suggestEmailCorrection(): the ONE email-domain typo suggester (hotmial.com, gmial.com, .con, .co.k) for every form that collects an address a receipt or access link is sent to. It only suggests; the page shows 'Did you mean x?' with accept and ignore.

resources.reason: a local UTM/click-id store is how this went wrong twice. One consumer lost two paid leads to a per-tab store and an internal link that overwrote the source; another wrote its own five-key sessionStorage capture inside a single page component and dropped fbclid and gclid entirely, so a site whose traffic is bought could not attribute a sale to an ad even in principle. The 90-day TTL, the consent gate, the paid-touch stickiness and the internal-link merge rule are each a fixed incident and none of them survive a re-implementation. Reading a stored value is fine; keeping your own store is not.

requestSignals.why: a pure classifier over request headers — it reads no table, calls no endpoint and holds no secret, so it owns no external resource. Its resources are deliberately empty rather than missing: the thing worth forbidding is not calling this function, it is BYPASSING the gate that calls it, and that is enforced on metaCapi's own match below because the bypass is written as a sendCAPIEvent call, not as a copy of this file. Extracted from metaCapi on 2026-09-10 so it could be tested at all — metaCapi imports server-only, which cannot resolve in the node:test build, and these rules are the ones stopping a costly incident from recurring.

device.why: a pure classifier over request headers (Client Hints + user-agent fallback) — no table, no endpoint, no secret, so it owns no external resource. Promoted here 2026-09-15 from the consumer site that first proved it, alongside pageEvents.ts (its main caller). The re-implementation risk this module exists to stop is not expressible as a resource match: enforced instead by scripts/check-classifier-tests.mjs, which requires any classifier of this shape (headers in, a small literal-string union out) to carry a committed, wired-in test — this file's own device.test.ts is that proof, and this repo's CI runs the gate on itself for exactly that reason.

resources.reason: the table is owned by the receiving app (a token-gated ingest route, via its own service-role client) — that route is the ONE legitimate writer and does not consume this module. Any OTHER repo writing to this table directly means it is holding a service-role key for a project it should not have one for, which is the exact indirection trackServerEvent()/the ingest endpoint exist to avoid. A sender site should never match this pattern in its own code at all — it only ever calls trackServerEvent(), which POSTs to the endpoint, never touches the table.

pageEvents.why: sends one aggregate, no-identifier funnel event (`landing` / `reserve_click` / `lead_submit`) to a shared ingest endpoint so consent-gated client analytics is not the only measurement of paid traffic. `site` is a caller parameter, never a constant. Deliberately reuses requestSignals' isAutomatedRequest and device.ts rather than re-checking either locally — see both modules' own why. Optionally carries a split-test assignment (`experiment` / `variant` / `experiment_forced`, from experiments.ts); a variant id is shared by many visitors, so the row stays aggregate-only.

consentEvents.why: browser-side trigger (`trackConsentEvent`) for the consent banner's `consent_shown`/`consent_accept`/`consent_reject` events (pageEvents.ts vocabulary) — added 2026-09-26 so the consent accept rate is a tracked metric instead of a one-off estimate. Owns no table or secret itself: it POSTs to whatever same-origin URL the caller gives it (the consumer's own route handler, which holds PAGE_EVENTS_TOKEN and calls trackServerEvent()). No resource match — the re-implementation risk is a hand-rolled fetch/sendBeacon call at the banner's Accept/Reject handlers instead of importing this module, which has no reliable textual signature distinct from an unrelated fetch call; enforced by review.

formEvents.why: the one contract for form-stage telemetry (`form_start`/`form_field_error`/`form_abandon`/`form_submit`, pageEvents.ts vocabulary) — added 2026-09-26 so every public form is diagnosable by construction, not just the one consumer that had it hand-built. `trackFormEvent` POSTs to the consumer's own same-origin route handler; `attachFormLifecycle` is the optional DOM-listener half for a plain form element. Owns no table or secret. No resource match — same reasoning as consentEvents: the risk is a hand-rolled per-form stage-event scheme, which is exactly what this module replaces and has no distinct textual signature; enforced by review.

posthogSessionRecording.why: a plain literal config object (masking defaults + the `data-ph-mask` selector convention) spread into a consumer's own `posthog.init()` call — it owns no external system and imports nothing, deliberately not even `posthog-js` types (golden rule 1b: posthog-js is not a dependency every web-core consumer installs). Added 2026-09-22 after estate issue 8e6fb948-935c-467b-bf9d-759d031bdb72 found all 12+ `posthog.init()` call sites across the estate had never set a `session_recording` or `enable_recording_console_log` option at all, so rrweb's factory defaults applied unchosen — 100% of checkout sessions recorded, console output captured, no client-side masking override. The project-level fix (URL blocklist, console opt-in, masking config) was made via the PostHog API directly and holds no place in this PUBLIC repo; this module is the client-side twin, set once so a future call site does not repeat the same unchosen default. No resource match: the re-implementation risk is a hand-typed `session_recording: { maskAllInputs: true, maskTextSelector: "..." }` literal inline at a call site instead of importing this module, which has no reliable textual signature distinct from a legitimate one-off override — enforced by review, same as consentBannerSize's convention-only entries. Rolling this into the 12+ consumer call sites is a separate estate-wide sweep, not done as part of adding the module — see the estate issue for the exact file/line list.

motion.why: scroll motion (reveal on entry, stagger, count-up) driven by data attributes, with its styles in motion.css. Owns no table, endpoint or secret. The duplication it replaces is per-site IntersectionObserver reveal hooks, each with its own threshold, class name and reduced-motion handling — not expressible as a resource match without firing on every legitimate IntersectionObserver use (lazy tracking, impressions). Enforced by review and the design standard instead.

clientEvents.why: browser-side GA4 `track()` and Meta `trackMeta()` (eventID dedupe + waitForConsent), plus the single-product param builders for both platforms. Owns no table, endpoint or secret: it calls `window.gtag`/`window.fbq` that the consumer's banner and adPlatforms loaded, and never loads a tag or decides consent itself. Promoted 2026-09-25 because every site hand-wrote the pair and the copies drifted on exactly the two details that make the numbers right: a missing eventID double-counts every consenting visitor against the server-side twin, and a load-time event that does not wait for consent is never sent. Not expressible as a resource match (a local `gtag("event", …)` call has no textual signature distinct from a legitimate one-off), so enforced by review and the scaffold's example wiring. Existing per-site copies are left alone: moving them is the per-site rollout, not this change.

resources.reason: a hand-rolled split-test buy-click route. The click endpoint (variant -> offer, exp/v passthrough, same-site referrer, the logged click, the trusted-host redirect) is createCheckoutClickHandler(); the site's route file is a one-line shim that passes its default offer and its event logger. Two sites each carried a copy of this route and they had already diverged (one resolved the variant's own offer for a price test, the other could not). Matches the COMBINATION: a funnel click logged without an experiment, or an order reading exp/v, is legitimate.
reading the split-test query params by hand skips the key/variant validation and the forced (QA) flag, so a malformed or forced view is counted as a real one. Use parseExperimentParams().
a cookie-carried split-test assignment needs consent, so it only ever measures the visitors who accepted cookies. Assignment is server-side and stateless (assignPageRequest / assignSticky).

experiments.why: THE split-testing module (server-side, cookie-free), one file so a plain `node --test` can load it: (1) config: validates an experiment config read live from the operator's token-gated endpoint (cached per instance, fail-safe to the control); (2) assignment: weighted, forced (`?v=`) or sticky-per-visitor pick, and assignPageRequest() for a page request (several tests per page, crawlers get the control, or the WINNER of a concluded test, never tagged) with the proxy->page header codec and experimentEventTag() (events logged under the path the visitor REQUESTED); (3) price tests: createVariantOfferResolver() maps variant -> offer -> that offer's own per-currency price rows, so the page price always equals the checkout price; (4) the buy click: createCheckoutClickHandler() is the whole `/go/checkout` route (variant's offer on the trusted checkout host only, exp/v/UTM/click-id passthrough, click event deferred). Reporting and auto-conclude live in the operator's reporting app, not here. Each site keeps only a thin shim (its site name, header name, default offer, event logger). The resources below flag the copies that existed before this was shared: a hand-rolled click route, hand-read exp/v params, a cookie assignment. A second offer-price reader is not matched here: the checkout app serves and embeds that endpoint legitimately, so it is registered only by the sites that run price tests.

resources.reason: the notification-centre ingest. A hand-rolled POST re-creates the never-throws contract, the base-URL safety check and the category vocabulary, and a drifted copy that swallows a 400 (unknown category) makes an alert vanish silently.

ccNotify.why: server-side producer for the central notification centre's token-gated ingest, for apps other than the receiver. The receiver owns rendering and whether a notification also emails or pushes; this module only raises it and reports whether it landed.

problemReport.why: the generic half of an in-app 'Report a problem': plain-text cleaning, coarse browser family (never the UA string), size-capped JSON snapshot fitting and the allow-listed client context (viewport, recent errors, Sentry id). Extracted 2026-09-26 from the first consumer's in-app report form so a second report form in any app never grows its own copy. Pure functions, no imports: it owns no table, bucket or endpoint (the consumer passes its own storage client, rate limits live in the consumer's DB trigger, replies go through supportTicket.ts, screenshots are validated with uploads.ts), so there is nothing a resource match could see. Enforced by its committed tests (problemReport.test.ts).

resources.reason: the issue tracker's bug-report ingest. A hand-rolled POST skips the allow-list cleaning (query strings and unknown client keys would reach the issue row), the never-throws contract and the base-URL safety check, and files issues whose steps and context read differently from every other app's.

bugReport.why: the server half of the staff 'Report a bug' button: cleans what the browser sent, maps it to issue-tracker fields (numbered steps to reproduce from the click/navigation trail, a context block) and forwards it with its pictures to the tracker's token-gated ingest. The React button lives in the shared app-shell UI repo (no React here).

cronPause.why: Reads one service-role RPC (`cron_control_check`) and writes the paused heartbeat THROUGH cronHeartbeat, which owns that write. No resource rule on purpose: the Command Centre's /agents admin screen legitimately reads and upserts `cron_controls` (the only writer), so a match on the table would fire on correct code. The Node twin for launchd/Paperclip agents is Barttech OS tools/cron-control.js — same table, same modes, same fail-open rule; change both together.
